descriptor: Regulated electric & gas utility holding company (New England) · Water Distribution divested June 2026 · FY ends 31 December · reported in USD

capexPlan.title: 5-year capital plan
capexPlan.content:
Each year's 10-K discloses a rolling 5-year forward capital expenditure plan, split between the Electric Transmission and Electric/Gas Distribution businesses.

For Eversource Energy: this plan, not reported revenue growth, is the core investment thesis -- a regulated utility earns an allowed return on the rate base its capital spend creates, so a rising plan ($23.1bn for 2024-28, $24.2bn for 2025-29, $26.5bn for 2026-30) is management's forecast of future earnings growth, subject to regulators approving the rate base into rates.

What to watch:

  • The plan growing vintage-over-vintage, not shrinking
  • Transmission vs Distribution mix -- transmission is FERC-regulated with formula rates and typically earns a more certain return than state-regulated distribution
  • Regulatory lag: capital spent today earns a return only once a rate case resets allowed revenue

customers.title: Total customers
customers.content:
Total customers is the sum of electric, gas and (through FY2025) water connections across Eversource's operating subsidiaries (CL&P, NSTAR Electric, PSNH, NSTAR Gas, EGMA, Yankee Gas, and Aquarion before its June 2026 sale).

For Eversource Energy: customer growth in a mature New England service territory is low-single-digit -- it is not the growth driver. The capital plan (and the rate base it builds) is; customer count mainly confirms the territory is stable, not shrinking.

What to watch:

  • Growth staying positive but slow (service-territory, not volume-growth, story)
  • Any subsidiary divestiture changing the total (Aquarion's ~249k water customers left the count after FY2025/mid-2026)

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue mix
segmentRevenue.content:
Revenue split across Eversource's regulated segments: Electric Distribution (the largest, retail electric delivery), Electric Transmission (FERC-regulated, formula-rate), Natural Gas Distribution, and (through FY2025) Water Distribution (Aquarion).

For Eversource Energy: Transmission is the smallest segment by revenue but usually the most predictable earner (formula rates, limited rate-case risk), while Distribution carries the bulk of both revenue and the capital plan. Water Distribution drops out of this chart after the Aquarion sale closed June 2026 -- a step-change in the mix, not a decline in the remaining businesses.

What to watch:

  • Transmission's revenue share rising with its larger share of the 5-year capital plan
  • Gas Distribution revenue swinging with winter weather and commodity pass-through, unlike the more stable electric segments
  • The FY2025-to-FY2026 step down when Water Distribution exits

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Eversource Energy: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Eversource Energy: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Eversource Energy: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Eversource Energy: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Eversource Energy: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Eversource Energy: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Eversource Energy: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Eversource Energy: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Eversource Energy: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Eversource Energy: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
